exam: A 7‑year‑old with bow‑legs, normal calcium and low phosphate – what is the next diagnostic step? — Order urine phosphate/creatinine ratio to confirm renal phosphate wasting.
How does FGF‑23 cause rickets? — It reduces proximal tubular phosphate reabsorption and suppresses 1‑α‑hydroxylase, leading to low phosphate and impaired mineralisation.
Distinguish hypophosphatemic rickets from nutritional rickets on labs. — Nutritional: low calcium, low 25‑OH D; Hypophosphatemic: normal calcium, low phosphate, high ALP, normal 25‑OH D.
Why is calcitriol preferred over cholecalciferol in treatment? — Calcitriol bypasses the blocked 1‑α‑hydroxylase step, directly increasing intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption.
What monitoring is essential after starting phosphate therapy? — Serum phosphate, calcium, ALP, and renal ultrasound for nephrocalcinosis every 3–6 months.
A child on phosphate therapy develops hyperphosphataemia and hypercalciuria – what should you do? — Reduce phosphate dose and reassess renal ultrasound; avoid calcium overload.
Explain why high-dose calcium supplements are avoided in this condition. — Excess calcium can precipitate with phosphate in kidneys, worsening nephrocalcinosis.
What feature on wrist X‑ray confirms rickets? — Widened, cupped metaphyses with frayed growth plate (rachitic changes).
ai.title: Hypophosphatemic Rickets
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A hereditary renal phosphate wasting disorder causing defective bone mineralisation. Presents with growth failure, bone pain and deformities, especially in low‑resource settings where diagnosis is clinical.

b: Low serum phosphate with normal/low 1,25‑dihydroxyvitamin D
Elevated alkaline phosphatase
Rachitic bone changes
sections.p: Hypophosphatemic rickets is a group of disorders characterised by renal phosphate loss, low serum phosphate, normal calcium, and inadequate bone mineralisation. The most common form is X‑linked (PHEX mutation).

b: FGF‑23 excess → phosphaturia
Impaired mineralisation of growth plates
Growth delay and limb deformities
sections.p: Pathophysiology centres on excess fibroblast growth factor‑23 (FGF‑23) which reduces renal phosphate reabsorption and suppresses 1‑α‑hydroxylase, leading to chronic hypophosphataemia.

b: History: progressive leg deformity, bone pain, fractures, family history
Exam: widened wrists, rachitic rosary, dental enamel defects, gait abnormality
Complications: nephrocalcinosis, secondary hyperparathyroidism, reduced height
sections.p: In East African hospitals children often present with bow‑leggedness, wrist pain and delayed milestones. Malnutrition and limited labs make clinical suspicion vital.
When FGF‑23 or urine studies are unavailable, rely on low serum phosphate with normal calcium, high ALP, and characteristic radiographs.

t.b: Is phosphate low? – Confirms phosphaturia; <2.5 mg/dL in children suggests disease
Is bone turnover high? – Markedly elevated in rickets
Are calcium and vitamin D normal? – Helps exclude nutritional rickets
Is renal phosphate wasting present? – Ratio >0.8 indicates phosphaturia
Is FGF‑23 elevated? – Supports diagnosis when labs are equivocal
Are growth plates widened and metaphyses cupped? – Radiographic hallmark

b: Oral phosphate supplements (multiple daily doses) to raise serum phosphate
Active vitamin D analogues (calcitriol) to enhance intestinal absorption
Monitor serum phosphate, calcium, ALP, and renal ultrasound regularly
Avoid high calcium intake that may precipitate nephrocalcinosis
sections.p: Treat the phosphate loss and support bone mineralisation while avoiding overtreatment that can cause nephrocalcinosis.

Renal osteodystrophy: usually secondary hyperparathyroidism with high phosphate
VDDR‑2: high 1,25‑D but end‑organ resistance, not FGF‑23 driven
sections.p: Nutritional rickets, renal osteodystrophy, and vitamin D‑dependent rickets type 2.
